title: Both Sides of the Aisle: Wait for the Floor, and for the Cash
web_title: 9. Bull vs. Bear, Portfolio Action & Redeployment Plan
book_title: Chapter 9: Bull vs. Bear, Likely Outcomes & Our Action Plan

epigraph.quote: “The margin of safety is always dependent on the price paid.”
epigraph.author: Benjamin Graham, The Intelligent Investor, chapter 20

web_blocks.html: Our call for new capital is WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT, with an accumulation zone of ₹40.00 to ₹42.00, an invalidation at a weekly close below ₹36.95, and a base value of ₹56. The business verdict from Chapters 1 to 6 is CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL with KPI health PASS_WITH_WATCH: a genuine, audited facade contractor whose profit is real and whose cash conversion is unproven. We use PASS_WITH_WATCH and not PASS because the order, margin and audit KPIs hold while the working-capital and cash-flow KPIs are weak, and not FAIL because H1 FY27 operating cash flow turned positive; a second weak half is what would turn the label, and the call, toward FAIL and REJECTED. The tape in Chapter 8 is Stage 4 with the timing gate CAP_REJECTED. The two statements fit together. The business is good enough to study and not yet good enough to chase, and the price is not low enough to ignore the cash question.

web_blocks.title: The strongest case for owning it

web_blocks.html: The bull case starts with visible work. Management reported an order book of about ₹300 Cr on 5 May 2026, which is about 2.2 times FY26 revenue of ₹138.6 Cr [2][1]. Individual orders are large and named: ₹89.9 Cr from Runwal over three years, ₹43.2 Cr for Godrej Reserve, ₹43.0 Cr from Vascon for a Capgemini campus and ₹23.8 Cr from L&T Realty for the Innovation Campus tower [17][14][16][12]. H1 FY27 operating margin before other income was about 13.4% on consolidated figures (13.5% standalone), up from about 12.3% (12.4%) a year earlier, and consolidated profit rose about 31% to ₹6.6 Cr [5]. The facade shop is described as close to full, and a ₹20 Cr extension adding 50 unitised panels a day is planned from the first quarter of FY28 [28].

Add the signs of better housekeeping. IPO money was used as stated with no deviation, the auditor's report is unmodified, and H1 FY27 operating cash flow turned slightly positive at ₹+0.8 Cr, with inventory down about ₹6 Cr in the half [1][5]. Shareholders approved a higher borrowing limit of ₹200 Cr with 100% of votes cast, which gives the company room to bid for larger orders [53]. The promoter holding edged up to 72.61%. At 9 times earnings and 1.45 times book, the stock is priced well below the 15.7 times of Ahluwalia and the 25 times of the new listing Glass Wall Systems [43][46][48]. If the cash cycle shortens, the re-rating is the whole upside case.

The bear case starts with the cash-flow statement. Operating cash flow was negative in FY24, FY25 and FY26, a total of ₹-37.5 Cr against ₹26.1 Cr of profit. Net trade working capital moved from about 41% of revenue to about 66%, borrowings rose from ₹13.1 Cr to ₹46.1 Cr in 18 months, and operating profit covered interest 9.1 times in FY25 and about 4.0 times in H1 FY27 [4][1][5]. The prospectus promised inventory of 72 days and payables of 27 to 29 days. FY26 delivered inventory near 207 days of materials consumed and payables near 144 days by our count (167 and 118 on the company's own ratio basis), so the working-capital plan behind the IPO was missed rather than delayed [3][1].

Then the guidance arithmetic. A ₹200 Cr FY27 means ₹126 Cr in the second half, 72% above the ₹73.1 Cr of H2 FY26, while the facade capacity is near full until mid-FY28 [5][28]. We put the probability of full delivery at 10% or less. The first-half profit gain also leaned on other income, which supplied about 83% of the rise in pre-tax profit over H1 FY26 and is not itemised in the filing [5]. Governance turnover is real: the company secretary resigned in May, the CFO in July, and an independent director in September 2026, with a new global-business president joining on 5 November [29][31][32][5]. The Eternia anchor agreement is due for renewal in December 2026 and Eternia-linked projects were 52% of FY24 H1 revenue [33][3]. The analogue in Chapter 7, Capacit'e, shows how this combination can end if collections slip.

The weighted gain of about 14% over roughly 18 months is thin for a stock with this liquidity and downside.

web_blocks.html: The weighted value of ₹51.3 sits 14.3% above the last close. That is about 9% a year, for a company where the bear case costs 39% and where the entry and exit may take days. At the last close the reward-to-risk to the base value, measured against the ₹36.95 invalidation, is 1.4 to 1, below our 1.5 to 1 hurdle. From the top of the accumulation zone at ₹42.00 it is 2.77 to 1 to the base value and 1.84 to 1 to the probability-weighted value, and from the bottom at ₹40.00 it is 5.25 and 3.70. The return hurdle matters as much as the ratio: at a 17% required annual return, the weighted ₹51.3 is worth paying only up to about ₹40.53 over 18 months, so the top of the zone earns about 14% a year, ₹41.00 about 16% and the bottom about 18%. Only entries at or below about ₹40.50 clear the hurdle, so we treat the bottom of the zone as the real entry and cap any purchase above ₹41, or before the H2 FY27 results, at one third of the 1,000-share limit. That is why the answer is a price-and-evidence wait and not a purchase at the last close or a rejection. About 80% of the base value is the multiple moving from 9.25 times to 11 times, so a stock that stays at 9.25 times is worth about ₹47 on the base earnings, and the call depends on cash evidence arriving to justify the re-rating. A rejection would be right if the business were failing the quality test. It is conditional because profit, margins and audit quality are intact, and the evidence that would settle the question arrives within six months.

How could this call be wrong? The cheapest error is waiting while the Eternia agreement is renewed and a large order lifts the stock 20% on thin volume; that costs about ₹9 a share against ₹44.90 and is a price we accept, because a stock trading 9,650 shares a day can gap past any limit and chasing it breaks the entry rule. The expensive error is buying into a break of ₹40 and averaging down while cash flow is still negative. That is why the invalidation is a weekly close below ₹36.95 and why a break leads to re-underwriting, not adding. An equity raise at a discount would also change the base case, as Capacit'e's 2023 raise did [51].

Two sensitivities let you test the table with your own inputs. Each ₹1 Cr of profit is about ₹0.40 of earnings per share on 2.48 crore shares, worth roughly ₹4.4 a share at 11 times. Each five points of revenue tied up in working capital is about ₹8 Cr on ₹165 Cr of sales, around 7% of the ₹110.6 Cr market value. For the owner, the cash cycle is worth more than the margin debate, which is why Chapters 6 and 7 spend their time there [43][5].

web_blocks.html: For a holder the question does not arise: the same-session positions ledger shows no ALUWIND shares, so the holding action is NOT_HELD with zero shares to sell. The alerts below are conditions for a future entry rather than instructions about an existing position. Any entry should be sized to liquidity first, about 1,000 shares or ₹45,000 at most, because the exit capacity of the stock is the binding limit; no more than one third of that before the H2 FY27 results, and only after the Eternia renewal is confirmed. These are advisory alerts, not broker orders [43].

Capital allocation comes last. We treat the next marginal cash unit as the capital under review and compare the choices. Aluwind earns 0% now because it is Stage 4 with the timing gate CAP_REJECTED and fails the entry hurdle at the last close; the table's stop column shows the snapshot's mechanical ₹43.50, while our 1.40 to 1 is measured to the structural ₹36.95, so it is not the same convention as the shortlist ratios. Two shortlist names clear the technical gate in the 13 November snapshot, Ajmera Realty (4.64 to 1 to its ₹195 base, Stage 2) and Manorama Industries (2.08 to 1 to its ₹2,650 base, Stage 2). We fund neither today. Ajmera was Stage 3 in the 12 November ledger, trades above the top of its own entry zone (₹133.28 against ₹132.17) and is already 4.06% of net worth in a real-estate name; Manorama also sits above its zone (₹1,984.10 against ₹1,957.58) after a 5.5% one-day fall from ₹2,100.10 that this dossier has not reviewed. No outside name is funded, and Aluwind stays the researched outside candidate at 0%. The whole unit therefore stays in cash until a setup clears the gates in a fresh snapshot.

web_blocks.intro: The risk-unit table converts the invalidation level into a share count for a portfolio risk budget. The call is a wait, so the displayed live allocation is zero; the scenario horizon is about 18 months (the FY28 results), and any purchase is capped at about 1,000 shares by liquidity.

web_blocks.html: Revisit the wait if the stock closes a week below ₹36.95 (abandon), if the Eternia agreement is not renewed or is narrowed, or if H2 FY27 operating cash flow is again negative with borrowings above ₹60 Cr. Upgrade to an accumulation plan if the price holds ₹40.00 to ₹42.00 and the renewal and cash-flow evidence arrive, or if a weekly close above ₹48.54 on 2x volume confirms Stage 2 with the cash evidence intact [33][5].

book_paragraphs: Let me tell you where I land, and then let us earn it. For new money, my call is wait: an accumulation zone of ₹40.00 to ₹42.00, an invalidation at a weekly close below ₹36.95, and a base value of ₹56. For the business itself, my verdict from the first six chapters is cyclical and conditional. It is a genuine, audited facade contractor whose profit is real and whose cash conversion is not proven. The chart is in Stage 4. Put those together and you get a business worth studying that you do not chase, at a price that does not yet pay you for the open question.

Let us give the optimist the floor first, as strongly as an optimist would. The company says it has about ₹300 Cr of orders in hand, 2.2 times last year's revenue. The orders have names you know: Runwal at ₹90 Cr, Godrej Reserve at ₹43 Cr, a Capgemini campus at ₹43 Cr, the Innovation Campus at ₹24 Cr. In the half-year to September, the operating margin rose to about 13.4% and consolidated profit grew about 31% to ₹6.6 Cr. The facade shop is almost full, and a ₹20 Cr extension for 50 more panels a day is planned from the first quarter of FY28 [2][17][14][16][12][5][28].

The optimist can also point to housekeeping that is improving. The IPO money was used exactly as promised. The auditor gave a clean opinion. In the first half of FY27, operations produced a small positive cash flow, and inventory dropped by about ₹6 Cr. Shareholders raised the borrowing limit to ₹200 Cr with every vote cast in favour, which gives the company room to take larger jobs. At nine times earnings and one and a half times book, the stock is priced below Ahluwalia at 15.7 times and well below the new listing Glass Wall Systems at 25 times. If cash catches up with profit, the whole upside case is a re-rating [1][5][53][43][46][48].

Now the pessimist, with the same courtesy. Over three years the company earned ₹26 Cr and its operations absorbed ₹37.5 Cr. Working capital grew from 41% of sales to about 66%. Borrowings rose from ₹13 Cr to ₹46 Cr in a year and a half. Operating profit covered interest nine times in FY25 and only about four times in the latest half. The prospectus promised 72 days of inventory and 27 to 29 days of payables. FY26 delivered about 207 days and 144 days by my count, or 167 and 118 on the company's own ratio basis, both far from the plan. That is a plan missed, not a plan delayed [4][1][5][3].

Then the guidance. The company wants ₹200 Cr of revenue in FY27. It has done ₹74 Cr in the first half, so the second half must deliver ₹126 Cr, 72% above last year's second half, while the facade capacity is near full until the middle of FY28. My probability that it hits the full number is 10% or less. A good part of the first-half profit gain came from other income, about 83% of the rise in pre-tax profit, and the filing does not itemise it. The company secretary, the CFO and an independent director all left within five months, and a new global-business president joined in November [5][28][29][31][32].

One more worry belongs on the table, because it is easy to miss. The Eternia anchor agreement, which makes Aluwind a preferred fabricator in the Mumbai region, expires in December 2026. Projects tied to Eternia were 52% of revenue in the first half of FY24. Nobody has announced non-renewal, and I assume renewal is likely. But the terms matter, and the company has not disclosed them. Chapter 7's Capacit'e story shows what happens when stretched cash meets a moment of stress [33][3].

How do I weigh the two cases? I give 35% to a bear year in which revenue reaches only ₹155 Cr and the stock is worth about ₹27. I give 45% to a base year of ₹190 Cr revenue and a stock near ₹56. I give 20% to a bull year of ₹215 Cr and about ₹84. The weighted value is about ₹51, which is 14% above the last close. That is roughly 9% a year for a stock where the bear case costs you 39% and where a large exit could take days. It does not pay me for the risk at ₹44.90.

Now look at the same trade through a stop. At ₹44.90, with a stop at ₹36.95 below the structural floor, the base value gives you 1.4 rupees of gain for every rupee at risk. My hurdle is 1.5. If you can buy at ₹42.00, it becomes 2.8 to 1, and lower it only improves. Against a 17% hurdle on the weighted value of ₹51, the break-even entry is about ₹40.50, so only entries near ₹40.50 or lower clear it, and above ₹41, or before the second-half results, I would buy no more than a third of my size cap. That is why my answer is a wait with a price and not a refusal. If the business were failing, I would reject it outright. It is not failing. Margins and audit quality are intact, and the evidence that settles the question will arrive within six months.

What are those pieces of evidence? First, whether Eternia renews in December. Second, the full-year results in about May 2027, which should show at least ₹5 Cr of operating cash flow in the second half, borrowings still below ₹60 Cr, and FY27 revenue near ₹165 Cr. Third, over the long run, whether the return on added capital rises above the 8% to 13.5% that the company pays its lenders, and whether the working capital falls toward half of sales. Those three tests cover the short, medium and long horizons, and today none of them is passed. I label the KPIs pass-with-watch and not fail because margins, orders and audit quality hold and the last half-year's cash flow turned positive; a second weak half would change that [33][5].

What about money you already own? The positions ledger shows no Aluwind shares, so there is nothing to sell, and the holding action is simply not held. If you do buy later, size it by liquidity first. About 1,000 shares, or ₹45,000, is the most I would hold, and no more than a third of that before the second-half results, because the stock's own trading volume is the binding constraint. Everything here is an advisory alert, not a broker order [43].

Let me test my own call by asking how it could be wrong. The most likely error is that I wait, the Eternia agreement is renewed, a good order arrives, and the stock jumps 20% in a week on thin volume. I would miss about ₹9 a share, roughly the gap between ₹44.90 and ₹54. I accept that risk. A stock that trades 9,650 shares a day can gap past any limit order, and chasing it would break my own rule about entry. The cost of being early to a mistake is usually larger than the cost of being late to a right call.

The other error is that the price drops through ₹40 before any good news, and I conclude the market knows something I do not. That is why the invalidation sits at a weekly close below ₹36.95 and not at a casual dip, and why I will re-underwrite rather than average down. The Capacit'e story from Chapter 7 reminds me that stretched cash cycles often end with an equity raise at a discount. If Aluwind announces one, I will treat it as new information about the base case, not as a bargain.

Two sensitivities help you check my arithmetic with your own numbers. First, each ₹1 Cr of profit is worth about ₹0.40 of earnings per share, because there are 2.48 crore shares, so at eleven times earnings each extra crore of profit is worth about ₹4.4 a share. Second, each five points of revenue tied up in working capital is about ₹8 Cr on ₹165 Cr of sales, which is around 7% of the whole market value. The cash cycle is worth more to the shareholder than the margin debate, which is why I keep returning to it.

And where should the next unit of cash go while Aluwind waits? I put all of it in cash. Two shortlist names, Ajmera Realty at 4.6 to 1 and Manorama Industries at 2.1 to 1, pass the technical gate in the 13 November snapshot. But the 12 November ledger had Ajmera in Stage 3, both sit just above the top of their own entry zones, Manorama fell 5.5% in a day that I have not reviewed, and Ajmera is already 4% of the portfolio in a real-estate name. I would rather wait for a fresh snapshot than fund a name on a conflicting reading. Aluwind gets 0%, with a price and a set of events that would change my mind. One caution on the numbers: my 1.4 to 1 for Aluwind is measured to my own ₹36.95 stop, while the shortlist ratios use the snapshot's closer stops, so they are not strictly comparable.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A wait is a decision. It says the business is worth owning at one price and not at another, and it names the evidence that would move the price. If the evidence arrives and the price is still there, you buy with a plan. If it does not, you have saved yourself the lesson.
